seo.title: Karmic tail 6 17 20 compatibility: what it means for a couple
seo.description: Karmic tail 6 17 20 compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Judgement. Why the middle is The Star, not Justice, and how Shakespeare's Pericles tells it.

title: The 6-17-20 karmic tail in compatibility: The Lovers, The Star and Judgement
short: The 6-17-20 couple's tail holds an oddity that needs no mysticism to see: Justice ought to stand in the middle, and The Star stands there instead. In a personal chart the middle is the sum of the two ends, 6 + 20 → 8. In a couple's chart it is put together differently and comes out as 17 — a number that hides the same eight in its digits: 1 + 7. This is the tail of a couple that enters its task by choosing each other (6, The Lovers), lives a long stretch of the road on hope and things left unsaid (17, The Star), and whose main task is to tell its own story aloud, among its own people, and to recognise each other anew (20, Judgement).

sections.h2: Why the middle is The Star, not Justice
paragraphs: In a personal destiny matrix the tail follows simple arithmetic: the middle is the sum of the ends. If 6-…-20 were a personal tail, the middle would be 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, Justice. That personal tail, 6-8-20, does exist in the method. A 6-17-20 tail never appears in a personal chart.

In a couple's chart each point is counted separately: the matching points of two personal charts are added together. The couple's middle comes from the partners' middles, not from its own ends. In nine couples out of ten with this tail, one partner's personal middle is 8, Justice, and the other's is 9, The Hermit. 8 + 9 = 17.

Add the digits and 1 + 7 = 8. That is no coincidence. Reducing a number by adding its digits never changes its remainder when divided by nine, so a couple whose ends are 6 and 20 can have only one of two middles: 8 or 17. This calculation allows no third option. Some couples carry the measure openly in the middle, as Justice. This couple carries the same measure hidden in the digits of The Star.

The difference between the two cards is the plot of the tail. Justice weighs: two pans, a tally, who owes whom how much. Waite gives its meanings as "Equity, rightness, probity". The Star does not weigh: its mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit", and among its readings is "hope and bright prospects". The 6-17-20 couple walks the middle of its road not by the tally but by hope: it gives, waits, trusts and does not check. That is its generosity. It is also its blind spot: when nobody weighs, nobody notices that the two have long been living not with each other but with an image of each other.

sections.h2: Pericles: a story told by a man risen from the dead
paragraphs: Around 1608 Shakespeare, together with the playwright George Wilkins, wrote Pericles, Prince of Tyre. The plot comes from a book that Europe, in the words of the Russian classicist Faddei Zelinsky, read for fourteen centuries — the anonymous late-antique History of Apollonius, King of Tyre — and from its retelling in a poem by John Gower, Chaucer's contemporary. Gower comes on stage himself as the narrator, and his first words are about resurrection: "To sing a song that old was sung, / From ashes ancient Gower is come". The play is told by a man who had died two hundred years before its premiere.

The play itself had a similar fate. Audiences adored it, yet Shakespeare's fellow actors left it out of the first collected edition of his plays in 1623. In 1629 Ben Jonson sneered at it as "some mouldy tale, / Like Pericles". It entered the collected works only in 1664, in the third edition, and for another century editors kept dropping it and bringing it back.

The story is simple. Pericles, ruler of Tyre, flees King Antiochus after solving his terrible riddle, is shipwrecked and lands in Pentapolis, where he wins a tournament and the hand of Princess Thaisa. On the voyage home, in a storm, Thaisa gives birth to a daughter and, as everyone believes, dies. Her body is laid in a pitch-sealed chest and thrown into the sea. The chest washes up at Ephesus, Thaisa is brought back to her senses, and she becomes a priestess in the temple of Diana. Their daughter Marina grows up in a stranger's house, and Pericles spends years in mourning. Fourteen years later the father finds his daughter, and in Diana's temple, his wife. The three movements run in the order of the tail: a choice, a long life on hope, a judgement and a resurrection.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: a father's armour and the motto "In this hope I live"
paragraphs: Pericles reaches Pentapolis with nothing: the sea has taken his ship and his men. Fishermen haul a rusty suit of armour out of the water in their net, and it turns out to be his dead father's. Dying, the father had told him: "Keep it, my Pericles; it hath been a shield / 'Twixt me and death". In that armour, rust and all, the son goes to the tournament for the princess's hand. The ancient source has no such scene — there the hero wins a ball game. The father's armour pulled from the sea is the play's own addition.

Before the joust the knights pass before Thaisa and show the devices on their shields. One carries a torch turned upside down and the motto "What feeds me puts me out". Pericles carries "A wither'd branch, that's only green at top" and the motto In hac spe vivo: "In this hope I live". The courtiers laugh at the rust. King Simonides, the bride's father, answers them: "Opinion's but a fool, that makes us scan / The outward habit by the inward man." One device holds the whole tail: the dry branch is the past and the inheritance, the green at the top is hope, and the knight hands his shield to the bride himself.

At the feast neither of them can eat. Pericles says the dishes "resist me, she but thought upon"; Thaisa finds every dish "unsavoury, / Wishing him my meat". To her he looks among the other knights "like diamond to glass". And Pericles looks at Simonides and sees his own father: "Yon king's to me like to my father's picture", who "Had princes sit, like stars, about his throne". The stars and the father — the other two cards of the tail — already sit at the table of love's feast.

When Simonides tells his daughter to ask who the knight is, Thaisa asks and then retells his answer to her father in her own words: the name, Tyre, the shipwreck. Lisovskaya writes that couples with The Lovers complete each other's stories beautifully. Here the couple's common language is born in exactly this way: she tells his story for him.

Then comes the letter. Thaisa writes to her father that she will "wed the stranger knight, / Or never more to view nor day nor light." The other suitors are told that the princess has vowed to wear "Diana's livery" for twelve more moons. Simonides stages a fit of anger, calls Pericles a traitor and ends like this: "Either be ruled by me, or I will make you — / Man and wife". The two answer together: "Yes, if it please your majesty."

Point M in a couple's chart stands for shared wishes and agreements, the couple's "common language". Here it is the wish to choose each other openly and beautifully, in front of their own people, and to be blessed. Wen writes of The Lovers: "there is a strong feeling of paradise, at least in the beginning." But M sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. The first thing Pericles says on reading the letter is: "'Tis the king's subtlety to have my life." Not long before, he had fled Antioch, where a beautiful bride turned out to be a riddle with a death sentence attached. Once burned, he sees a trap in the gift. Among the tasks of a couple with The Lovers, Lisovskaya names insecurity, from which jealousy and control grow, and dependence on relatives. In this couple it looks like this: love is so wanted that it is frightening to believe in, and the two people's "yes" is spoken in the father's voice.

One more detail of the entry. The excuse made to the suitors — a year in Diana's service — will later become fourteen years of Thaisa's life. In the play, words said at the entry "for show" become the rule in the middle. A couple with this tail would do well to look at its own first words — about freedom, about "we don't need anyone", about "breaking up is easy" — and check whether they have quietly become law.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: fourteen years on a single hope
paragraphs: The storm catches the ship as Thaisa is giving birth. The nurse brings out the baby and tells Pericles: "Patience, good sir; do not assist the storm." Pericles answers the gods: "Why do you make us love your goodly gifts, / And snatch them straight away?"

Then the sailors come: the sea "will not lie till the ship be cleared of the dead". "That's your superstition," says Pericles. "With us at sea it hath been still observed: and we are strong in custom." And he gives way: "As you think meet." Not because he believes them, but because someone else's custom has proved stronger. Thaisa is laid in a pitch-sealed chest with jewels and a letter: whoever finds her should give her burial, for "She was the daughter of a king".

At Ephesus the chest is opened by Cerimon, a lord who has spent his life studying herbs and stones. The first thing he says is: "They were too rough / That threw her in the sea." And then: "Death may usurp on nature many hours, / And yet the fire of life kindle again / The o'erpress'd spirits." He calls for music, and Thaisa opens her eyes: "Where am I? Where's my lord? What world is this?"

Now the heart of the middle. From the letter Thaisa knows that her husband survived that night: it is his handwriting. And she decides: "since King Pericles, / My wedded lord, I ne'er shall see again, / A vestal livery will I take me to, / And never more have joy." Pericles, leaving his daughter at Tarsus, swears that his hair shall stay "Unscissor'd" until she marries, "Though I show ill in't". Years later, at his daughter's false tomb, he puts on sackcloth, swears never to wash his face, and for three months speaks to no one. Gower, standing by that tomb, tells the audience: "See how belief may suffer by foul show!"

Two people keep faith with each other, and neither checks. He never once doubts her death. She never once writes to Tyre, although a king is not hard to find. Each makes a vow alone, and each vow is a picture of loyalty that the other cannot see.

This is The Star in the middle, both its sides. For Lisovskaya, The Star in a couple is a union that inspires both partners, and the rare case where the beautiful picture is true. Its shadow is the same picture with nothing inside, and things left unsaid. In the play the shadow is not vulgar: nobody shows off. But instead of a conversation the two have a picture: a tomb, a priestess's robes, uncut hair. Waite opens The Star's list of meanings with "Loss, theft, privation, abandonment" — and the middle of the play goes through all four literally: the wife is lost at sea, the daughter is stolen by pirates, the father refuses food and speech, the child is left in a stranger's house.

The middle of a couple's tail is our reading of how the couple travels from the wish of M to the task of D. The 6-17-20 couple travels it on hope. It may be a long stretch: work in another city, a child, a move, caring for parents. Each protects the other and keeps quiet about the hardest things. Both are faithful — and both are lonely. The measure is there inside, the very eight hidden in the digits of seventeen, but nobody takes it out.

In the fifth act Pericles looks at an unknown girl, not yet knowing she is his daughter, and says: "thou look'st / Modest as Justice, and thou seem'st a palace / For the crown'd Truth to dwell in". Justice and Truth in one line — 8 and 17, the measure and The Star. Both old Russian translations lost Justice: Pyotr Kanshin has "as modest as pravda", Pavel Kozlov "modest as holy truth". In Russian the loss barely shows: in Old Russian pravda meant both truth and law — the law code of Yaroslav the Wise is called Russkaya Pravda. A measure hidden inside truth — like an eight hidden inside seventeen.

sections.h2: The couple's atmosphere: a death that turned out to be sleep
paragraphs: The tail is read together with the rest of the couple's chart. In 91% of couples with the 6-17-20 tail the centre of the chart — the sphere "The atmosphere inside the couple" — holds 13, Death. In 6.7% it is The Emperor, in 2.4% The Fool.

Waite calls Death "more especially a card of the death of Kings", and writes that "the alternatives allocated to the symbol are change and transformation". In Pericles kings die one after another: Antiochus with his daughter, Pericles's father whose armour came up from the sea, and finally Simonides. And two living people are buried: Thaisa in the sea, Marina in a tomb at Tarsus. Pericles says of his daughter: "Thou that wast born at sea, buried at Tarsus, / And found at sea again!" And of her too: "thou dost look / Like Patience gazing on kings' graves, and smiling / Extremity out of act." The Star gazes at the graves of kings — the middle of the tail gazes at the centre of the chart.

Wen notes that The Star "appears chronologically in the Major Arcana after a great deal of pain: The Hanged Man, Death, The Devil, and The Tower." This couple is built the same way: the hope of the middle grows right beside Death in the atmosphere. Inside the union one can clearly hear that everything ends. Hence the couple's strength — the ability to let go of what has truly ended — and its main danger: mistaking sleep for death. A quarrel for a break-up, a cooling for an ending, a pause for a grave. Cerimon puts it more precisely than any reading: death may rule for a long while, and still the fire kindles again.

sections.h2: Main task: telling everything in front of everyone
paragraphs: Act five. Pericles's ship lies off Mytilene. He himself lies behind a curtain; for three months he has spoken to no one, nor taken food "But to prorogue his grief". They bring him a girl who sings — Marina. He does not hear. She speaks to him, and he pushes her away. She says she has endured a grief that "Might equal yours, if both were justly weigh'd" — the scales again. She wants to leave, but something "whispers in mine ear, 'Go not till he speak.'"

Step by step: her name is Marina. Why Marina — because she was born at sea. Her mother died the minute she was born. Pericles cannot believe it, asks to be struck "Lest this great sea of joys rushing upon me / O'erbear the shores of my mortality", and at last: "O, come hither, / Thou that beget'st him that did thee beget". And at once: "Give me fresh garments."

The play has an exact architecture. It opens in the palace of Antiochus with a riddle in which one and the same man is "father, son, and husband": a family whose every boundary has been erased by violence. It closes with a line of the same shape: a daughter who gives birth to her father. The roles change places again, but now through a gift, not a crime. The American Shakespeare scholar C. L. Barber took this line as the title of his 1969 essay.

Then Pericles hears music. "The music of the spheres! List, my Marina." — "My lord, I hear none." He alone hears the summons that Waite describes for Judgement, one that "is heard and answered from within". In a dream Diana appears to him and tells him to sail to Ephesus and there, "Before the people all", to "Reveal how thou at sea didst lose thy wife". The ancient source has the same: the goddess orders Apollonius to tell his fate aloud before her altar.

In the temple Pericles tells everything: who he is, how he married, how his wife died at sea in childbirth, how his daughter grew up and nearly died. The high priestess faints: "Voice and favour!" Then: "Like him you spake, / Like him you are: did you not name a tempest, / A birth, and death?" Thaisa recognises her husband by his story. Pericles still argues: "I threw her overboard with these very arms." A moment later: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." The same arms, the same verb: a burial becomes an embrace. Thaisa's proof is a family one — the ring her father gave Pericles. And straight away comes the news: "My father's dead." Pericles answers: "Heavens make a star of him!" The last star of the play is a dead father, and the couple will live out their days in his kingdom.

For Lisovskaya, Judgement is the card of lineage and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. Pericles has all of it, and all of it decides the couple's fate. The father's armour was a shield against death. The father's game blessed the marriage. The sailors' custom proved stronger than love. Marina's foster mother, Dionyza, cannot bear that the girl outshines her own daughter — comparison, The Star's shadow, lives here among relatives. The father's ring proves who is who, and in the end the couple inherits the father's kingdom. Lisovskaya reads point D mainly through its minus, and her tasks for a couple with Judgement are these: to admit mistakes; to manage to say what one feels and what one dislikes; to find boundaries — such couples tend to have either none at all or impenetrable ones. In the play Antiochus has no boundaries at all, while Pericles's three months of silence are impenetrable. The way out is a full account in front of witnesses.

For the couple, the main task of Judgement arrives as a summons: a moment comes when silence is no longer possible. The whole story has to be told — to each other and to their families — with the losses, the mistakes and whatever each has already buried alone. Waite's divinatory meanings for Judgement are "Change of position, renewal, outcome", and in the play the renewal can be seen: fresh garments, the vow lifted, and the hair that "this fourteen years no razor touch'd" trimmed for the daughter's wedding. In Wen, Judgement reversed means the Seeker "has misinterpreted the facts or evidence presented and has arrived at the wrong conclusion". The play's main mistake is exactly that: both believed in a death neither of them saw. On the plus side, Lisovskaya's Judgement means forgiving mistakes, and the way everything lived through together binds a couple. Pericles tells the gods in the temple: "your present kindness / Makes my past miseries sports". The past does not vanish. It becomes a story that can be told.

sections.h2: Waite and Wen: a star in the lantern and coffins on the water
paragraphs: A few more pieces of evidence lie in the drawings of Waite's deck — by Pamela Colman Smith — and in how Waite and Wen describe them. These are drawings from their deck, not the cards on our site.

Of The Hermit, Waite writes: "It is a star which shines in the lantern." And he quotes the old explanation that The Hermit "is said to be in search of that Truth which is located far off in the sequence, and of Justice which has preceded him on the way." In the Marseille order our site uses, Justice, 8, stands immediately before The Hermit, 9. Waite himself disagrees: for him this is "a card of attainment" rather than "a card of quest". But the couple's arithmetic repeats the old reading: in nine couples out of ten the middle is built from one partner's Justice and the other's Hermit, and the sum is The Star, whose figure, Waite says, will appear to "the majority of prepared minds" as "the type of Truth unveiled".

Wen compares The Star with Temperance: both show a figure at the water, but in Temperance "there is a balancing", while The Star "depicts a pouring out in one direction". That is the difference between 8 and 17 in the middle: scales with two pans, and a jug that pours without expecting anything back.

Of Judgement, Wen writes of "the body of water that the coffins float upon", and she assigns the card to the element of Water. In Shakespeare, Thaisa's coffin is a pitch-sealed chest on the waves, which the sea itself carries to the shore.

And one word links the entry and the middle. Waite's Lovers are "two human figures, male and female, unveiled before each other", and the figure of The Star is for him "Truth unveiled". First the two are open to each other. Then they have to open up before the truth. And in the finale — before everyone.

sections.h2: How the 6-17-20 tail looks in a couple's life
paragraphs: Lisovskaya advises reading a tail in links between cards and saying, for every conclusion, which combination it follows from. The 6-17-20 tail has four such links.

ul: **The Lovers and The Star (6 + 17).** A love that is pleasant to look at. Such partners often discover who they want to be precisely within the couple, and help each other open up. The shadow is the one beautiful photographs have: the picture of happiness takes the place of life, comparisons with other couples begin, and the waiting for an ideal.

**The Star and Judgement (17 + 20).** Hope against family. They wait a long time: until the relatives accept them, until there is a home of their own, until one partner is ready for the child the other already wants. Each carries the hardest part alone. The plus of this link is the ability to forgive and start again after a long stretch.

**The Lovers and Judgement (6 + 20).** A choice made under the eyes of the family. Parents bless the union or withhold their blessing, and the couple needs to tell its own choice apart from someone else's custom — to say, as Pericles said to the sailors, "That's your superstition", but this time not to give way.
**All three cards (6 + 17 + 20).** A story told aloud. At the start the two tell each other's stories, in the middle they keep silent, at the end they have to tell everything — among their own.

paragraphs: What it looks like in daily life. They have known each other a month and already tell their friends each other's story better than their own. Then comes a long period when each protects the other and keeps quiet. Sometimes, after a hard quarrel, one of them silently puts up a gravestone over the relationship — "that's it, it's over" — while the other, in a temple of their own, vows never to be happy again. The main task arrives not as a catastrophe but as a conversation: to sit down and tell everything in order, the tempest, the birth and the death, without embellishment.

This is not a forecast. The tail says nothing about events or dates, or about who is right and who is to blame. It shows a plot two people may recognise in themselves — and the place where that plot turns.

sections.h2: What helps a couple with the 6-17-20 tail

ul: **Checking before burying.** Before deciding "it's all over", asking: what did I see myself, and what did I simply believe? Thaisa recognised her husband's handwriting and still put on a priestess's robes.
**Saying aloud what was sworn in silence.** A silent vow of loyalty is a picture the other cannot see. Spoken, it becomes an agreement that can be discussed.

**Telling someone else's custom from one's own decision.** Relatives, traditions, "this is how we do things" — all of it deserves respect and is worth passing on, but decisions about the couple are made by the two.

**Not living inside a picture.** Not comparing each other with an ideal or with other couples, not standing in the way of the partner's dream, and not forcing a choice between the partner and their work.
**Marking the end of a hard time.** Pericles had his hair trimmed for his daughter's wedding. A couple, too, benefits from a visible sign: the waiting is over, ordinary life begins.
**Telling their story together.** First to each other — in full, with the losses and the mistakes. Then, if needed, to their families.

sections.h2: The strong version of the tail
paragraphs: The strong 6-17-20 couple is the one that can tell its story to the end. In it the storm becomes a chapter, not the finale. Such partners recognise each other by voice and by story, as Thaisa recognised Pericles. Their choice was blessed, then held for a long time on a single hope, and it all ends not in resignation but in recognition.

Shakespeare's ending gathers the whole tail. A father made into a star — Judgement, turning the past into light. Marina, "Modest as Justice" — the measure hidden inside The Star. The arms that threw her into the sea are the same arms that embrace.

The couple's values — its spiritual purpose — are most often The Empress (45.7%), The World (36.7%) or The Hanged Man (17.6%) in such couples. To our reading, the play's ending holds all three: a mother to whom her daughter returns — "Flesh of thy flesh, Thaisa"; two kingdoms and a whole sea, from Tyre to Ephesus; and fourteen years of a life suspended between hope and mourning. This is our reading, not a rule of the method.

sections.h2: How to calculate the 6-17-20 couple's tail: an example
paragraphs: The example is a couple born on 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1976.
First partner: day 14, month 9, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 5 = 22. Karmic task: 14 + 9 + 22 = 45 → 9. Centre: 14 + 9 + 22 + 9 = 54 → 9. Tail entry: 9 + 9 = 18, middle: 18 + 9 = 27 → 9. Personal tail: 18-9-9.

Second partner: day 14, month 10, year 1 + 9 + 7 + 6 = 23 → 5. Karmic task: 14 + 10 + 5 = 29 → 11. Centre: 14 + 10 + 5 + 11 = 40 → 4. Tail entry: 4 + 11 = 15, middle: 15 + 11 = 26 → 8. Personal tail: 15-8-11.
The couple's tail is the sum of the matching points:

Check: 6 + 20 = 26 → 8, yet the middle is 17. The couple's middle is not recalculated from its ends; it is added up from the partners' middles. The couple's centre in this example is 9 + 4 = 13, Death, and the couple's values are 3, The Empress.
The 6-17-20 tail occurs in roughly one couple in 121 (0.825%) and ranks 44th of the 97 couple tails. It is formed by four combinations of the partners' personal tails:

Four different roads lead to the same Star: Justice and The Hermit (8 + 9), The Emperor and Death (4 + 13), The Empress and Temperance (3 + 14), The Wheel of Fortune and The Chariot (10 + 7). The Star is in none of these personal tails: only the couple puts it together.

ul: **6 · The Lovers — entry to the task.** The couple's shared wish: to love openly and beautifully, to choose each other and to hear a "yes" from their families. The same impulse can turn into resistance — when it is frightening to believe the gift is real.

**17 · The Star — middle of the task.** How the couple walks its road: on hope, generously, without weighing. In its shadow, a beautiful picture instead of a conversation, and vows each partner makes in silence.

**20 · Judgement — main task.** Lineage, family, inheritance and the ability to admit a mistake. The main test is to say aloud what has been carried inside for years — and not to bury what is still alive.

intro: What follows is an investigation. There are three kinds of evidence: arithmetic that does not match the personal chart; the books of Waite, Benebell Wen and Yuliana Lisovskaya; and Shakespeare's play Pericles, whose three movements run exactly in the order of this tail — a tournament and a wedding, fourteen years apart, a recognition in a temple.

faq.q: What does the 6-17-20 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: These are the couple's tasks in the order "entry — middle — main task". The entry is The Lovers: the wish to choose each other openly and with the blessing of their families. The middle is The Star: a road travelled on hope and generosity, where it is easy to replace a conversation with a beautiful picture. The main task is Judgement: lineage, family, admitting mistakes and the ability to tell one's story aloud.

faq.q: Why is the middle 17 if 6 + 20 gives 8?
faq.a: In a couple's chart the middle of the tail is not calculated from its ends. It is added up from the middles of two personal tails, most often 8 + 9 = 17. Reducing by digits keeps the remainder when divided by nine, so with ends of 6 and 20 the middle can only be 8 or 17 — and the digits of seventeen add up to the same eight.

faq.q: Does the 6-17-20 tail mean the couple will break up?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events, dates or break-ups, and it does not say who in the couple is right. It describes a task: not to live for years on a single hope and silent vows, but to check, to speak and to recognise each other anew.

faq.q: Does the 6-17-20 tail occur in a personal matrix?
faq.a: No. In a personal matrix the middle of the tail equals the sum of its ends, and with ends of 6 and 20 the tail would be 6-8-20. The order 6-17-20 is possible only in a couple's chart. There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 6, 17 and 20 either.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether they have the 6-17-20 tail?
faq.a: By calculating the compatibility matrix from the two birth dates: find each partner's personal tail, then add their matching points and reduce any sum above 22. In the example above, 14.09.1975 and 14.10.1976 give 18 + 15 → 6, 9 + 8 = 17 and 9 + 11 = 20.

report: In Shakespeare's Pericles a husband throws overboard, with his own hands, the coffin of a wife who is still alive — and then keeps faith with her for years. Fourteen years later he says to her: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." Between these two gestures lies the whole 6-17-20 tail: choosing each other, a long life on a single hope, and recognition.

The tail's oddity shows in the numbers themselves. In a personal chart the middle is the sum of the ends, and here it would be 6 + 20 → 8, Justice. In a couple's chart the middle is added up from the middles of two personal tails, and it comes out as 17, The Star. The digits of seventeen hide the same eight: 1 + 7. **This couple has a measure, but it is hidden inside The Star.** Justice weighs: two pans, a tally, who owes whom how much. The Star does not weigh: its mottoes are "Waters of Life freely" and "Gifts of the Spirit". The 6-17-20 couple walks the middle of its road not by the tally but by hope — it gives, waits, trusts and does not check.

report.h3: A love that begins with someone else's story

report: The entry to the task is The Lovers: the shared wish to choose each other openly, beautifully and with the blessing of their own people. Pericles comes to the tournament for Princess Thaisa's hand in his dead father's rusty armour, which fishermen hauled out of the sea in their net. On his shield is "A wither'd branch, that's only green at top" and the motto "In this hope I live". The courtiers laugh at the rust, and the king, the bride's father, answers: "Opinion's but a fool, that makes us scan / The outward habit by the inward man."

When the king tells his daughter to ask who the knight is, Thaisa retells his answer to her father in her own words. This is how the couple's common language is born: **she tells his story for him.** But the entry sits on the line of tasks, and the same wish turns into resistance. On reading her love letter, Pericles says: "'Tis the king's subtlety to have my life." Once burned, he sees a trap in the gift. Love is so wanted that it is frightening to believe in, and the two people's "yes" is spoken in the father's voice: the king stages a fit of anger and ends by declaring them man and wife.

report.h3: Two loyalties the other knows nothing about

report: The middle of the task is The Star. A storm, a birth, and Thaisa is taken for dead. The sailors demand that the body go overboard. Pericles calls it superstition — and gives way all the same: someone else's custom has proved stronger. On another shore the chest is opened, and the first words spoken over it are: "They were too rough / That threw her in the sea." Thaisa opens her eyes, recognises her husband's hand in the letter — and decides: "since King Pericles, / My wedded lord, I ne'er shall see again, / A vestal livery will I take me to, / And never more have joy." Pericles swears not to cut his hair, puts on sackcloth at his daughter's false tomb and for three months speaks to no one. The play's narrator remarks: "See how belief may suffer by foul show!"

Two people keep faith with each other, and neither checks. **Each makes a vow alone, and each vow is a picture of loyalty that the other cannot see.** This is The Star in the middle: hope and generosity, and in its shadow a beautiful picture instead of a conversation, and things left unsaid. In a couple's life it is a long stretch — work in another city, a child, a move, caring for parents — when each protects the other and keeps quiet about the hardest things. Both are faithful — and both are lonely.

Later Pericles will say to an unknown girl, not yet knowing she is his daughter: "thou look'st / Modest as Justice, and thou seem'st a palace / For the crown'd Truth to dwell in". Justice and Truth in one line — the eight and The Star. This couple's main danger is mistaking sleep for death: a quarrel for a break-up, a cooling for an ending, a pause for a grave. The play says it more precisely than any reading: "Death may usurp on nature many hours, / And yet the fire of life kindle again / The o'erpress'd spirits."

report.h3: The main task is to tell everything in front of everyone

report: The main task is Judgement, the card of lineage and family: relatives, traditions, inheritance, the influence of parents. It is read above all through what fails: admitting mistakes, saying what one feels, keeping boundaries — such couples tend to have either none at all or impenetrable ones.

It is his daughter who brings Pericles out of his silence. He recognises her step by step and at last says: "O, come hither, / Thou that beget'st him that did thee beget". Then he alone hears music, and the goddess tells him to reveal, "Before the people all", how he lost his wife at sea. In the temple he tells everything, and the high priestess faints: "Voice and favour!" **Thaisa recognises her husband by his story** — by the tempest, the birth and the death. Pericles still argues: "I threw her overboard with these very arms." A moment later: "O, come, be buried / A second time within these arms." The proof is the ring her father gave Pericles. And straight away comes the news of that father's death. Pericles answers: "Heavens make a star of him!"

For a couple with this tail, Judgement arrives as a summons: a moment comes when silence is no longer possible. The whole story has to be told — to each other and to their families — with the losses, the mistakes and whatever each has already buried alone.

report.h3: Hands that buried learn to embrace

report: Simple things change the script. Checking before burying: what was seen, and what was merely believed. Saying aloud what was sworn in silence: a silent vow is a picture the other cannot see, a spoken one is an agreement that can be discussed. Telling someone else's custom from one's own decision: relatives and traditions deserve respect, but decisions about the couple are made by the two. Marking the end of a hard time — Pericles had the hair that "this fourteen years no razor touch'd" trimmed for his daughter's wedding.

The strong 6-17-20 couple is the one that can tell its story to the end. **In it the storm becomes a chapter, not the finale.** Such partners recognise each other by voice and by story, and the past does not vanish — it becomes a story that can be told. In the temple Pericles tells the gods that their present kindness turns his past miseries into sport.
